turns.text: How do other organisations use dembrane, and how should I set up my first project?

The practitioners in this project use dembrane for citizens' assemblies, planning drop-ins, staff listening, offsites, research interviews and even a family care decision. For a first project, their advice comes down to six habits.

1. Write the project context as a briefing: who is in the room, the questions per round, what is already decided and what is still open, and local names as key terms. (Coaching call before a first 40-person evening; Ministry analyst onboarding a new colleague)

2. Decide privacy before anyone records. Agree the legal basis and whether to anonymise transcripts; anonymising removes names but also switches off audio playback. (Privacy officer, works council and project lead agree the rules)

3. One phone per small table, and test it. Keep groups to three to six, screens on with Do Not Disturb, scan the QR code on your own phone first, and have someone watch the Monitor for locked screens. (Town centre day, the blunt retrospective; Festival crew retro, 52 tables in the tram depot)

4. Name conversations so you can find them later: use the name field as a round and table label, like "R2 T09", and set tags per round. (Member network general assembly to roadmap, peer phone call)

5. Tidy before you analyse, then ask for disagreement. Delete tests and empty rows, ask what only one table said, where tables disagreed and who was missing, and open every source. (Two analysts rebuild a flood plain report)

6. Bring it back to the people who spoke. Read a draft aloud and record the room's corrections, and copy quotes from transcripts, never from a chat answer. (Reading the draft back to the room; Sceptical councillor, committee pre-meeting)

Tell me what you are planning and I'll find the conversations closest to it.
